newsitem.title: USA: Perry's comments stir behind-scenes anguish.
newsitem.headline: Perry's comments stir behind-scenes anguish.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Perry is an articulate spokesman for U.S interests but officials say he sometimes gives the Clinton administration heartburn with comments that go beyond official rhetoric.
Does Perry have a "tin ear" for how his comments sound, as some speculate, or does he assert himself deliberately in order to exercise greater influence over policy?
Officials outside the Pentagon say the point is debatable.

"My perception is that Perry feels this administration doesn't really have someone in charge of foreign policy and he feels he has to step into that breach," said Lawrence Korb, a former defence official now with the Brookings Institution.

"Sometimes he gets out front. Sometimes he forces action" and serves U.S. interests, Korb said in an interview. "This can create problems for American diplomacy because when the administration is not speaking with one voice, you send mixed signals and this undermines our credibility."
In the most recent example, Perry seemed to escalate U.S. warnings of imminent, devastating retaliation against Iraq when he threatened the use of "disproportionate" force.
Then, his department apparently jumped the gun by announcing last Friday that 5,000 more U.S. troops would be sent to Kuwait before the Kuwaiti government gave final approval to the plan.

Several weeks ago, Perry raised eyebrows -- at a time when the administration was trying to be vague on the issue -- by indicating publicly that NATO would have to deploy some kind of follow-on force when its troops leave Bosnia in December.

He also created a stir when he publicly suggested, before an investigation was completed, that Iran was linked to the June 25 bombing of an U.S. military housing complex in Saudi Arabia that killed 19 servicemen and wounded 250.

Such comments have caused eyes to roll in the State Department and the White House. Although there has been no hint of serious presidential displeasure with Perry he has been urged to alert the administration before he speaks on sensitive matters.
The Pentagon declined to comment directly on this story but one Pentagon spokesman told Reuters: "Look at the secretary's words and the president's words and they are virtually interchangeable."
But many officials comment, albeit anonymously, about what they see as the Perry puzzle.
"He is the best internal player in the administration and his record is superb as defence secretary in terms of operations," one official said, adding: "But he happens to be a loose cannon."
Another official, asked about Perry's penchant for rhetoric that is more muscular or forward-leaning than U.S. policy, replied: "It happens over and over again. People have talked to him about it."
One explanation, some suspect, is that Perry is not a politician and so speaks his mind without appreciating how his words will reverberate domestically and internationally.
But that seems an odd excuse for a highly experienced senior official who is considered among the brightest and most capable members of President Bill Clinton's cabinet.

Perry, 68, was defence undersecretary from 1977-81 and is considered the father of the stealth technology that helps aircraft evade radar detection. He worked in private industry before returning to the Pentagon as deputy secretary in 1993.
"I don't think Perry ever misstates policy," said one official. "But there are times when the way he phrases it causes the possibility of us boxing ourselves in."
Perry's reference to using "disproportionate" force at a key point in the showdown with Iraqi President Saddam Hussein was not vetted by Clinton's senior national security advisers.

Some officials outside the Pentagon fretted that Perry's choice of words gave the impression Washington was committed to quickly launching another attack on Iraq that would inflict far more damage than earlier missile strikes.
In fact, Washington was prepared to strike but also was ready to step back from confrontation if Saddam did likewise.
Both sides retreated. But Perry's threat lingered, leaving a sense of dissonance and giving Republicans a chance to critize Clinton for seeming to vacillate.
In Perry's defence, one analyst said: "Bill's directness sometimes gets him into trouble but he's a highly principled man, one of the few straight-shooters in government."
